name: Assumption audit
intent: Surface the beliefs the plan silently rests on.
when: before committing, or when something keeps failing for unclear reasons
prompt: List what has to be true for this to work. Mark confidence: ●+ high, ◐~ medium, ○! unsure.
readback: Every assumption marked low and untested is a risk. The cheapest way to check it is the next physical action.

claims.claim: Explicitly listing the assumptions a plan depends on, and naming a test for each, identifies more of the plan's vulnerabilities than reviewing the plan without such a list.

Coarse, three-level confidence ratings discriminate correct from incorrect judgements above chance (resolution), even though people are typically overconfident in absolute terms. Items marked low-confidence are therefore a useful flag for risk.
Asking people to consider reasons their judgement could be wrong reduces overconfidence and biased assimilation, compared with no instruction or an instruction to be unbiased.

grounding.helps: when a plan rests on beliefs nobody has written down; listing assumptions is practitioner craft with no direct test, and the evidence that asking for a reason each could be wrong reduces overconfidence is mixed, so treat the low-confidence dots as a guide to which to test first, not a correction
grounding.backfires: when the falsifier column asks for many reasons against each assumption, since listing many is hard and can strengthen the original belief, or when a high-confidence dot is read as proof, because certainty runs ahead of accuracy
